questions.q: Why must human-centred design solutions keep adapting after launch?
options: Because people and their needs are dynamic and changing
questions.explain: Measure effectiveness against the original aims and keep improving.
questions.evidence: HCD recognizes that people and their needs are dynamic and changing, and so solutions must also adapt to changing needs.

questions.q: What is human-centred design (HCD)?
options: A qualitative research method to solve problems with solutions that put customer needs ahead of a system's needs
A way to design attractive logos
questions.explain: It starts from people's real needs, not the organisation's processes.
questions.evidence: Human-centered design (HCD) is a qualitative research method that helps groups solve problems and seek solutions that prioritize customer needs over a system’s needs.

questions.q: How should you think of an HCD discovery?
options: As the final step of a project
As a straight line from start to finish
As a cycle, not a linear process
questions.explain: Each round of learning sends you back to refine questions.
questions.evidence: Think of HCD discovery as a cycle, instead of a linear process.

questions.q: What is participatory design?
options: Letting the most senior person decide
Giving participants an active role in the life cycle of the work
Asking users to pay for the design
Designing alone, then presenting to users
questions.explain: Participants act as equals to the design team and leadership.
questions.evidence: Giving participants an active role in the life cycle of our work is sometimes called participatory design.

questions.q: What happens in the solution implementation step of the design process?
options: The final concept options are selected and carried through to completion
questions.explain: Implementation turns the chosen concept into finished designs.
questions.evidence: we are ready to select the final concept options and carry their application through to completion in producing the final design(s).

questions.q: In a design studio session, what should you remind participants about sketching?
options: Anyone can draw — artistic accuracy is not the goal
questions.explain: Quick, rough sketches let everyone contribute ideas.
questions.evidence: Remind them that anyone can draw and artistic accuracy is not the goal of the exercise.

questions.q: Why should you map a user's whole problem?
options: To find more users to charge
Because what you are working on is probably part of a bigger task users are trying to complete
questions.explain: Mapping shows how the journey is delivered today and where to improve it.
questions.evidence: This is because what they’re working on is probably part of a bigger task that users are trying to complete.

questions.q: Who are the creative thinkers, according to 'Words of Wisdom'?
options: Those who always pick option A
Those who invent solution C while everyone else argues between A and B
Those who copy the best existing answer
questions.explain: Creative and critical thinking work together.
questions.evidence: They are the ones who invent solution C when everyone else is still arguing between A and B.

questions.q: What must you do before committing to build anything?
options: Make prototypes to explore, share and test different designs
questions.explain: Prototypes are cheap ways to learn what works.
questions.evidence: You must make prototypes of your service to explore, share and test different designs before you commit to building anything.

questions.q: How should prototypes be, according to the 18F method?
options: Quick and painless to create — and even quicker to discard
questions.explain: Low-cost prototypes make it easy to throw away ideas that don't work.
questions.evidence: Prototypes should be quick and painless to create, and even more quick and painless to discard.

questions.q: How do the phases of the human-centred design process relate to each other?
options: They can be done in any order
They are sequential, but the process as a whole is cyclical
They all run at the same time
questions.explain: Learning from later phases feeds back into new discovery.
questions.evidence: These phases are sequential, but the process as a whole is cyclical.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the HCD design guides?
options: To list every design process that exists
To share select methods for solving the problems found in discovery
questions.explain: They are a starting point, not an exhaustive list.
questions.evidence: The purpose of these guides is to provide context and share some select methods for designing products, services, and systems that will help solve the problems highlighted from your discovery phase.

questions.q: What does defining goals allow a designer to do?
options: Home in on exactly what to communicate and who the audience is
questions.explain: Clear goals guide every later design decision.
questions.evidence: Defining goals allows you to home in on precisely what to communicate and who the audience is.

questions.q: What did research reveal about millennials and advertising?
options: They respond best to fear-based ads
They resist negative advertising, so messages should be positive and realistic
They only respond to celebrity endorsements
questions.explain: Knowing this before concept development shapes the message.
questions.evidence: Research also reveals that millennials resist negative advertising

questions.q: In visual communication, how is meaning expressed?
questions.explain: Messages carry both intellectual and emotional meaning.
questions.evidence: Meaning is expressed not only through content but through form as well

questions.q: What is a concept in communication design?
options: A list of the client's requirements
The typeface chosen for a project
An idea that presents key messages in interesting, unique and memorable ways
questions.explain: Good concepts work on intellectual and emotional levels.
questions.evidence: A concept is an idea that supports and reinforces communication of key messages by presenting them in interesting, unique, and memorable ways on both intellectual and emotional levels.

questions.q: Which 1960s campaign is given as an early example of a strong concept?
questions.explain: Its witty, playful idea made a small car's size a selling point.
questions.evidence: Volkswagen Beetle (VW) advertising campaign of the 1960s

questions.q: Why is design called an iterative process?
options: It repeats the same design for every client
It builds content and details by critiquing the work as it develops
It is done in a single pass
questions.explain: Critique at each stage tests the design against the concept and problem.
questions.evidence: Design is an iterative process that builds the content and its details through critiquing the work as it develops.

questions.q: What is concept development?
options: Developing ideas to solve specified design problems
questions.explain: Concepts move from formless idea to a precise message in an appropriate form.
questions.evidence: Concept development is a process of developing ideas to solve specified design problems.

questions.q: What differentiates a designer from a production artist?
options: The creativity to develop effective, appropriate concepts
questions.explain: Production artists execute; designers conceive the idea.
questions.evidence: The creativity that helps develop effective, appropriate concepts is what differentiates a designer from a production artist.

questions.q: Besides being creative, what must a good concept be?
options: Appropriate for its audience and purpose
questions.explain: It must motivate the audience to take action.
questions.evidence: A good concept is creative, but it also must be appropriate.

questions.q: When mapping concepts, how should early ideas be treated?
options: Every possible concept is valuable and should not be judged yet
questions.explain: Judging too early shuts down creative exploration.
questions.evidence: At this stage, every possible concept is valuable and should not be judged.

questions.q: In communication design, what is allusion?
options: A brief, informal reference to a well-known person or cultural item
Expanding on an idea in detail
questions.explain: Rhetorical devices add layers of meaning to a concept.
questions.evidence: Allusion is an informal and brief reference to a well known person or cultural reference.

questions.q: What is amplification as a rhetorical device?
options: Expanding on an idea so the audience realises its importance
questions.explain: It adds weight to the key point of a message.
questions.evidence: Amplification allows you to expand on an idea to make sure the target audience realizes its importance.

questions.q: Why should what a team builds fit into the user's wider journey?
options: Because every service must be a single page
So each team can work in isolation
It is probably part of a bigger task the user is trying to complete
Because users only do one thing at a time
questions.explain: Mapping the whole problem keeps the journey user-centred from start to finish.
questions.evidence: is probably part of a bigger task that users are trying to complete

questions.q: How can mapping a user's whole problem help delivery teams?
options: It helps prioritise what they should work on next
It removes the need for testing
It lets them skip the alpha phase
questions.explain: The map shows where the biggest gaps in the journey are.
questions.evidence: What you discover can help you prioritise what delivery teams should work on next.

questions.q: What is a lo-fi way of finding organisations involved in a user's problem?
options: Look on GOV.UK for organisations publishing content on the subject
questions.explain: Published content reveals who already works on each part of the journey.
questions.evidence: A lo-fi way of doing this is to look at GOV.UK to see which organisations are publishing content on relevant subjects.

questions.q: Which question does Baker suggest asking to think critically about information?
options: Does it agree with my view?
What is the source of this information?
questions.explain: Purposeful, frequent questioning sharpens critical thinking.
questions.evidence: What is the source of this information?

questions.q: Why are code prototypes better for user research than sketches?
questions.explain: They can look and behave like the live service.
questions.evidence: Code prototypes are better for user research because they

questions.q: What are sketches useful for?
options: Exploring and discussing basic ideas with colleagues
questions.explain: Use the prototype that best meets your needs at the time.
questions.evidence: Sketches are useful for exploring and discussing basic ideas with colleagues.

questions.q: Should you keep prototyping once a service is in beta or live?
options: Yes — to explore new features and improvements
No, prototypes are only for discovery
questions.explain: Prototyping stays cheaper than building the wrong thing.
questions.evidence: Continue to use prototypes in the beta and live stages of your service to explore potential new features or improvements.

questions.q: Which of these does a prototype NOT need to do?
options: Look realistic enough for user testing
Be easy to share with the team
Be secure and handle large volumes of traffic
questions.explain: A prototype only needs to support learning, not production use.
questions.evidence: For example, it does not need to be secure or to perform well with large volumes of traffic.

questions.q: Like a wireframe, what should an early prototype focus on?
options: Structure and relationships between elements, not styling
questions.explain: Prototypes should be quick to create and even quicker to discard.
questions.evidence: demonstrate structure and relationships among different elements, but don't worry about stylized elements

questions.q: What is the first step in forming a design hypothesis?
options: As a team, identify and make explicit the problem you are solving
questions.explain: A hypothesis links that problem to a change you expect to make a difference.
questions.evidence: identify and make explicit the problem
